n: With the temple finished, Solomon gathers Israel’s leaders to bring the ark of the covenant from David’s tent in the City of David up to the new temple on the higher hill.

f.w: the ark of the covenant of the LORD

f.g: Here the original City of David, just south of the temple mount.

n: All Israel assembles during the great autumn festival in the seventh month — the Feast of Tabernacles, which celebrated God’s care in the wilderness.

f.g: The seventh month (September–October), later called Tishri.

n: The elders arrive, and the priests lift the ark — this time carried properly, as the law required.

f.w: the priests took up the ark

n: The priests and Levites bring up the ark, along with the old tabernacle of Moses and its sacred vessels, which were now stored in the temple.

f.g: The tent of meeting from Moses’ day, which had been at Gibeon.

n: Solomon and the people offer countless sacrifices as the ark proceeds — an outpouring of worship.

f.w: could not be told nor numbered

n: The priests place the ark in the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the great cherubim.

f.w: under the wings of the cherubims

n: The cherubim’s outstretched wings overshadow the ark and its carrying poles.
The poles are so long that their ends can be seen from the Holy Place, though not from outside. They remained there “unto this day” — when this account was first written.

f.w: there they are unto this day
f.g: Showing the source was written while the temple still stood, before 587 BC.

n: Inside the ark were only the two stone tablets of the covenant that Moses placed there at Sinai (Horeb).
As the priests leave, a cloud fills the temple — the same visible sign of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle in Moses’ day.

f.w: the cloud filled the house of the LORD

n: The glory of the Lord is so overwhelming that the priests cannot continue their service. God has accepted His house.
Solomon speaks: the Lord said He would dwell in thick darkness — the cloud that both reveals and veils His presence.
He declares he has built a lofty house for God, a settled dwelling place forever.

f.w: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever

n: Solomon turns to face the standing congregation and blesses them.
He praises God, who promised David with His mouth and fulfilled it with His hand — God’s word and deed always match.
Since the Exodus, God had not chosen a city for His house; instead He chose David to lead His people.
Building a temple had been David’s heart’s desire.

f.w: it was in the heart of David

n: God commended David for that desire, even though He did not let him build it. God honors righteous desires of the heart.

f.w: thou didst well that it was in thine heart

n: Instead, David’s son would build it.
God has kept His word: Solomon is king and the house is built.

f.w: the LORD hath performed his word

n: Solomon has made a place for the ark, which holds the covenant God made with Israel at the Exodus. The temple is a house of covenants.

f.w: wherein is the covenant of the LORD

n: Solomon stands before the altar, facing all Israel, and lifts his hands toward heaven to begin his great dedicatory prayer. Latter-day Saints may notice similar themes in the Kirtland Temple dedicatory prayer.

f.w: spread forth his hands toward heaven

n: He begins with praise: no God is like the Lord, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who walk before Him wholeheartedly.

f.w: there is no God like thee

n: God has kept His promise to David — again, spoken by His mouth and fulfilled by His hand.
Solomon asks God to keep the rest of His promise: a descendant on David’s throne, provided his children walk faithfully.

f.w: There shall not fail thee a man

n: He asks God to confirm His word to David.

A profound question: can God truly dwell on earth? Even the highest heavens cannot contain Him — how much less this building? The temple does not confine God; it is a place where heaven and earth meet.

f.w: the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee

n: Still, Solomon humbly asks God to listen to his prayer and plea today.
He asks that God’s eyes be open toward this house day and night, where His name dwells, and hear prayers offered toward it.
The key refrain of the prayer begins: “Hear thou in heaven… and forgive.” The temple is a place to seek forgiveness and reconciliation with God.

f.w: hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place
f.g: This phrase repeats throughout the prayer, stressing that God truly dwells in heaven.

n: First case: when someone is accused of wronging a neighbor and swears an oath of innocence at the altar.

f.w: an oath be laid upon him

n: Solomon asks God to judge justly — condemning the guilty and vindicating the innocent.

f.g: Declaring the innocent to be in the right.

n: Second case: when Israel is defeated in battle because of sin, but then repents and prays at the temple.

f.w: because they have sinned against thee

n: May God forgive and restore them to their land.

f.w: bring them again unto the land

n: Third case: drought caused by sin. If they pray, confess, and turn from sin, Solomon asks God to respond.
May God forgive them, teach them the right way to live, and send rain. Forgiveness leads to learning to walk in God’s ways.

f.w: that thou teach them the good way

n: Fourth case: any disaster — famine, plague, crop disease, locusts, siege, or sickness.

f.g: Crop blight caused by scorching winds.
Probably a stage of the locust.

n: When anyone, aware of “the plague of his own heart,” prays toward this house — the personal sense of sin and need — Solomon asks God to hear.

f.w: the plague of his own heart
f.g: One’s own inner sorrow or sin.

n: May God forgive and deal with each person according to their heart, which only He truly knows.

f.w: thou, even thou only, knowest the hearts

n: Then the people will revere God all their lives in the land He gave them.
Fifth case: a foreigner who comes from far away because of God’s reputation. The temple is meant to bless all nations, not Israel alone.
They will hear of God’s great name and mighty acts and come to pray toward this house.
Solomon asks God to answer the foreigner’s prayer so that all peoples may know and revere Him. Jesus later called the temple “a house of prayer for all nations.”

f.w: that all people of the earth may know thy name

n: Sixth case: when Israel goes to battle at God’s direction and prays toward Jerusalem and the temple.
May God hear and uphold their cause.
Seventh case: when Israel sins — and everyone sins — and God allows them to be taken captive to a foreign land. This proved prophetic of the later Assyrian and Babylonian exiles.

f.w: there is no man that sinneth not

n: If in captivity they come to their senses, repent, and confess their sins, Solomon asks God to listen.

f.g: Come to their senses; take it to heart.

n: If they turn back with all their heart and soul and pray toward their land, city, and temple — as Daniel later did in Babylon — God will hear.

f.w: pray unto thee toward their land
with all their heart, and with all their soul

n: May God hear their prayer from heaven and uphold their cause.
May He forgive them and move their captors to show them compassion — as later happened under Cyrus of Persia.

f.w: give them compassion before them who carried them captive

n: For they are God’s own people, whom He rescued from Egypt, that furnace of suffering.

f.g: A smelting furnace — an image of Egypt’s harsh bondage.

n: Solomon asks God to keep His eyes open and His ears attentive to all their prayers.
God set Israel apart from all nations as His own inheritance, as He said through Moses. This covenant relationship is the basis of the whole prayer.
Solomon rises from kneeling before the altar with hands raised to heaven. A king kneeling before God shows where true authority lies.
He stands and blesses the whole congregation in a loud voice.
He praises God for giving Israel rest; not one of His good promises through Moses has failed.

f.w: there hath not failed one word of all his good promise

n: He prays that God will be with them as with their ancestors and never abandon them.

f.w: let him not leave us, nor forsake us

n: He asks God to turn their hearts toward Him so they will keep His commandments. True obedience comes when God changes the heart.
May these prayers remain before the Lord day and night, so He will help His servant and people as each day requires.
The ultimate goal: that all peoples of the earth will know that the Lord is God and there is no other.

f.w: that the LORD is God, and that there is none else

n: Solomon charges the people: let your hearts be fully devoted to the Lord. Sadly, Solomon himself would later fail to keep this charge.

f.w: Let your heart therefore be perfect

n: The king and all Israel offer sacrifices before the Lord.
Solomon offers an enormous number of peace offerings — shared meals of fellowship that likely fed the vast crowd over the festival. The temple is formally dedicated.

f.w: dedicated the house of the LORD
f.g: Dedicated = consecrated, set apart for holy use.

n: Because the bronze altar is too small for so many offerings, Solomon consecrates the middle of the courtyard as an additional place of sacrifice.
A massive celebration follows, with people from the far north (Hamath) to the Egyptian border, lasting two weeks: seven days of dedication and seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles.

f.w: the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt
f.g: From Israel’s northern frontier in Syria to the Wadi el-Arish in the south.

n: Afterward Solomon sends the people home. They bless the king and leave joyful, grateful for all God’s goodness to David and to Israel. This is a high point of Israel’s history.
